title: Beatrix and the Compass
premise: In the winter of 1899, during a colonial war few at home wish to name, Emrys Brightwater works as a battlefield nurse, quietly recording in a hidden ledger the names of soldiers whose deaths officers erase to protect reputations and promotions. When an unknown child is abandoned at the infirmary door with a note reading 'forget the face,' Emrys realizes the boy is the son of a massacred regiment—and living proof of what really happened. Pursued by Major Corvane, the officer who ordered the cover-up, Emrys must smuggle the ledger and the child past three military checkpoints before New Year's Eve, when Corvane's promotion will seal the records forever. The journey costs Emrys their anonymity, an old friendship, and nearly their life, but ends with the testimony delivered and Corvane undone—not by violence, but by the simple, stubborn act of remembering.
about_author: Zephyrine Eriksen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military correspondence from forgotten colonial campaigns. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Emrys Brightwater's POV. In a muddy field hospital, Emrys tends the wounded by day and records erased names by night, establishing their careful invisibility and quiet moral fury. Emotional beat: weary resolve—the reader learns what it costs to notice what others are paid to forget.

chapters.title: A Knock After Curfew
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A soldier Emrys once treated leaves a sleeping child at the infirmary door with a note: 'forget the face.' Before Emrys can question him, he's reassigned to the front. Emotional beat: dread blooming into reluctant responsibility.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wouldn't Speak
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The child, Tomas, refuses to talk but clutches a regimental button from a unit officially 'never deployed.' Emrys cross-references the ledger and finds forty omitted names. Emotional beat: the first cold certainty that this is evidence, not charity.

chapters.title: Major Corvane Inspects the Infirmary
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, with Corvane's polished menace on full display. The major tours the hospital, praising efficiency while his eyes catalogue faces. He mentions, casually, that a child was reported missing from a burned village. Emotional beat: fear sharpened into performance—Emrys lies well for the first time.

chapters.title: Sister Agnes Knows
chapters.summary: Sister Agnes's POV. The head nurse, who has survived three wars by seeing nothing, reveals she saw everything—including where Emrys hides the ledger. Instead of betraying them, she offers the hospital's supply route as a smuggling path. Emotional beat: unexpected solidarity between two kinds of survivors.

chapters.title: What the Button Belonged To
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. A dying sergeant confirms the massacred regiment was ordered to hold a position that was never reinforced—on Corvane's written command. He asks Emrys to add his name to the ledger while he can still dictate it. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints, One Night
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Planning chapter: the river checkpoint, the rail yard, and the governor's gate must all be crossed before December 31st, when Corvane's commission makes the records legally untouchable. Emotional beat: tense clarity—a map drawn in candle smoke.

chapters.title: The Friend Who Counts Names Differently
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Hale's POV. Emrys's oldest friend, now Corvane's adjutant, discovers the ledger's existence and faces his own arithmetic: loyalty versus conscience. He warns Emrys without reporting them—but takes the ledger's duplicate key. Emotional beat: betrayal shadowed by love.

chapters.title: Flight Through the Laundry Line
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Soldiers search the infirmary; Emrys smuggles Tomas out in a linen cart, abandoning the only home and identity they've built. Emotional beat: terror laced with exhilaration—invisibility is over, and part of Emrys is relieved.

chapters.title: The River Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. First crossing: a bribed ferryman, a forged pass, and a patrol boat's searchlight. Emrys hides Tomas among cargo barrels and talks their way past a young sentry who looks like every boy in the ledger. Emotional beat: guilt and luck entangled—one checkpoint down.

chapters.title: Tomas Speaks
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV, rendered spare and childlike. On the road, the boy finally speaks, describing the night soldiers came to his village and the man with the silver whistle who gave the order. Emotional beat: devastating innocence—the child becomes witness, not burden.

chapters.title: Hale at the Rail Yard
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Hale's POV. Second checkpoint: Hale is posted at the rail yard, knowing Emrys must come through. He finds them, hesitates, and lets them board the freight car—but reports a 'false sighting' to buy time, sealing his own ruin. Emotional beat: sacrifice disguised as paperwork.

chapters.title: Corvane Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Major Corvane's POV. The major interrogates Sister Agnes, burns the infirmary's records, and issues shoot-on-sight orders for a 'kidnapper and stolen child.' We see his self-justifying logic: order requires forgetting. Emotional beat: chilling banality of corruption.

chapters.title: Snowbound
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Stranded in a shepherd's hut by a storm, Emrys and Tomas wait out two days, sharing stories and rations. Emrys confesses why they keep the ledger—a brother whose death was filed as 'desertion.' Emotional beat: tenderness and trust forged in stillness.

chapters.title: The Shepherd's Price
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The shepherd who sheltered them is arrested for aiding fugitives. Emrys must choose: rescue him and miss the deadline, or go on. They send word to Agnes instead, trusting the network they've built. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh—survival always bills someone.

chapters.title: The Governor's Gate
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Third checkpoint: the capital's gate on December 30th, thick with holiday traffic and Corvane's men checking every cart. Emrys sews the ledger pages into Tomas's coat lining and walks through openly, betting that boldness reads as innocence. Emotional beat: white-knuckle triumph—through, but exposed.

chapters.title: An Old Debt in the Capital
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys seeks a retired judge, once saved by Emrys's nursing, who agrees to hear testimony—but warns that witnesses alone won't hold against Corvane's patrons. They need the original muster rolls. Emotional beat: hope complicated by the machinery of power.

chapters.title: What Hale Carried Out
chapters.summary: Lieutenant Hale's POV. Arriving half-frozen, Hale delivers the original muster rolls he stole from Corvane's office, along with the confession that he signed the false deployment report. He surrenders himself to the judge. Emotional beat: redemption purchased at the price of career and freedom.

chapters.title: New Year's Eve
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Corvane, tipped off, comes for Tomas personally at the judge's house. In the confrontation, Emrys reads the ledger aloud—name after name—while Corvane's own soldiers stand listening, recognizing brothers among them. Emotional beat: climax; memory itself becomes the weapon.

chapters.title: The Silver Whistle
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The child identifies Corvane by the whistle around his neck, produced as evidence alongside the muster rolls. Corvane's patron withdraws protection rather than be tainted; the major is taken into custody as the year turns. Emotional beat: catharsis—power undone by its smallest witness.

chapters.title: Forty-One Names
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The inquiry opens; the ledger is entered into record, each name read into the public transcript. Hale awaits sentencing with unexpected peace; Agnes rebuilds the infirmary; the shepherd is released. Emotional beat: bittersweet vindication—justice arrives late and incomplete, but it arrives.

chapters.title: Beatrix and the Compass
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV, one year later. Emrys has adopted Tomas, taking the surname Beatrix from their mother, and keeps a new ledger—this time of the living. The compass that guided their flight hangs by the door, pointing not north but home. Emotional beat: belonging earned, survival paid for, memory kept.
